answer.rationale: Rollback (memory_b1) is off the table: compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so the single most-precedented fix is unavailable regardless of how well it worked on day 18. The degradation is confined to the primary region, which points at a regional fault rather than the release, and memory_b2 is the only inherited record of a region-confined latency fix. That is exactly why it needs verification rather than reuse: the March event it describes recovered 'latency and error rates,' which are read-visible metrics, and the record says nothing about whether the shifted traffic was write-heavy or whether replication lag was checked afterward. Our primary objective explicitly forbids losing customer writes, and a failover at settlement peak with heavy writes can satisfy the latency metric while silently dropping or duplicating in-flight writes — the failure mode that would be invisible in the very dashboards that made memory_b2 look like a clean success. So I spend the single verification pull on memory_b2 to learn the write profile and whether replication lag was bounded. Hence the small guarded test: shift a bounded slice of write traffic to the secondary, hold it, and gate expansion on a write-integrity check (reconciliation of the shifted slice, replication lag, no gaps in settlement sequence) rather than on p99 alone. If the archived record shows March was read-dominated or that lag was never verified, memory_b2 does not transfer to this situation and I fall back to route_read_replicas (memory_b5), which cannot lose writes and plausibly relieves primary contention, accepting that it may be insufficient. add_capacity (memory_b3) was preventive headroom provisioned before a peak, not a mid-incident remedy, and will not land in 90 minutes; enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) addressed a failing external partner dependency, and shedding writes here would directly violate the no-write-loss constraint. Downstream risk flagged: a latency-only 'success' here would consolidate into memory as further proof that failover-first is correct, compounding a metric that omits write integrity and biasing future agents toward the same blind spot; whatever I record must state the write-integrity result explicitly, including if it was not measured.
